walkthroughs.body_html:
Environmental & Ecological Economics — a core area of Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Environmental & Ecological Economics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Environmental & Ecological Economics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The benefits people gain from nature, such as pollination and clean water, are called:
options: Ecosystem services
Externalities
Natural income
Market goods

mcqs.q: Pollution from a factory that harms residents but is not reflected in its prices is an example of an:
options: Externality
Ecosystem service
Subsidy
Natural capital stock

mcqs.q: The world's stock of natural resources viewed as economic assets is termed:
options: Natural capital
Gross domestic product
An externality
Carrying capacity

mcqs.q: The 'polluter pays' principle states that the cost of pollution should fall on:
options: Those who cause it
The general taxpayer
Future generations
No one at all

mcqs.q: What is a negative externality in environmental economics?
options: A cost imposed on third parties not reflected in the market price, such as pollution.
A benefit the producer keeps for themselves.
Because natural capital refers only to money in banks.
A tax charged on all businesses.

mcqs.q: Why can natural capital be 'used up' even though nature renews itself?
options: Because natural capital refers only to money in banks.
GDP only measures pollution levels.
Because harvesting beyond the natural income depletes the underlying stock faster than it regenerates.
Because natural capital is completely unlimited.

mcqs.q: Does GDP fully measure a country's environmental wellbeing?
options: Yes; GDP captures all environmental costs.
GDP only measures pollution levels.
A tax charged on all businesses.
No; GDP ignores resource depletion and pollution, so it can rise while natural capital falls.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Natural capital”?
options: A cost or benefit of an economic activity that falls on third parties and is not reflected in market prices, such as pollution from a factory.
The world's stock of natural resources and ecosystems, such as forests, soils and fisheries, regarded as assets that yield goods and services.
The idea that those who produce pollution should bear the costs of managing it to prevent damage to human health or the environment.
The benefits people obtain from ecosystems, such as clean water, pollination, climate regulation and recreation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Natural income”?
options: The sustainable yield of goods or services that natural capital can provide without depleting the underlying stock.
A cost or benefit of an economic activity that falls on third parties and is not reflected in market prices, such as pollution from a factory.
The idea that those who produce pollution should bear the costs of managing it to prevent damage to human health or the environment.
A method of weighing the total expected costs of a project against its benefits, including environmental impacts, to inform decisions.
